title: Change, perspective and responsibility
summary: How behaviour changes and how we study change, how different perspectives explain the same behaviour, and the ethical responsibilities of psychologists.

keyterms.definition: How behaviour, cognition or the brain develops or is altered over time, and how researchers measure this.
Research that follows the same participants over a long period to track change.
Research comparing different groups (e.g. ages) at one point in time.
A particular point of view or level of explanation (biological, cognitive, sociocultural) used to explain behaviour.
Explaining complex behaviour by breaking it down into simpler parts or a single level, e.g. genes or neurotransmitters.
Explaining behaviour by looking at the whole person and the interaction of many factors.
Studying a culture from the inside, using concepts meaningful to its members.
Studying cultures from the outside using concepts assumed to apply universally, allowing comparison.
Participants agree to take part after being told what the study involves; parents consent for under-16s.
Explaining the true aims to participants after the study, especially after deception, and checking their well-being.
Participants can leave the study and remove their data at any time without penalty.
Misleading participants about the aim or procedure; only acceptable when necessary and followed by debriefing.
Replacement, reduction and refinement: principles for ethical animal research (Russell & Burch, 1959).
The duty to consider how findings could be used or misused in society, and who could be harmed.

questions.prompt: Which design is best for studying how one group of children's memory changes from age 5 to 15?
questions.explanation: Following the same children over time shows change within individuals.

questions.prompt: A disadvantage of longitudinal studies is that:
options: They compare different people at one time
questions.explanation: Attrition can bias the remaining sample if those who leave differ from those who stay.

questions.statement: A cross-sectional study comparing 10-year-olds and 20-year-olds may confuse age differences with cohort (generation) differences.
questions.explanation: The groups grew up at different times, so differences may reflect experience, not age.

questions.statement: Explaining depression only in terms of serotonin is an example of holism.
questions.explanation: Reducing depression to one neurotransmitter is biological reductionism.

questions.text: Explaining behaviour from the viewpoint of members of the culture being studied is an ___ approach.
questions.explanation: Emic research uses insiders' own concepts; etic research applies outside, supposedly universal ones.

questions.text: Breaking behaviour down into one simple level of explanation is called ___.
questions.explanation: Reductionism can make research testable but ignores interacting factors.

questions.prompt: Match each perspective to an explanation of anxiety.

pairs.right: Learning fear from family and cultural norms

questions.explanation: Using several perspectives gives a fuller explanation than any single one.

questions.prompt: Hofstede's cultural dimensions apply the same measures to every country. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Applying common dimensions across cultures is etic; it allows comparison but may miss local meanings.

questions.prompt: Which is a strength of biological reductionism?
questions.explanation: Reducing behaviour to measurable variables makes it testable, but may oversimplify.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a typical longitudinal study.
items: Recruit a sample and take baseline measures
Re-measure the same participants at intervals
Track attrition and compare those who stay with those who leave
questions.explanation: The defining feature is repeated measurement of the same people.

questions.prompt: In Milgram-style studies where participants are misled about the aim, which ethical step is most essential afterwards?
questions.explanation: Debriefing reveals the deception, explains the aims and checks participants leave in the state they arrived in.

questions.prompt: A 14-year-old wants to join a study. Who must also give consent?
options: The ethics committee instead of the child
questions.explanation: For minors, parental consent is needed, and the child should also agree (assent).

questions.statement: Participants should be able to withdraw their data even after the study has finished.
questions.explanation: The right to withdraw includes removing one's data, e.g. after debriefing.

questions.statement: Deception is never allowed in psychological research.
questions.explanation: Mild deception can be justified if the study could not work otherwise, no significant harm is expected and participants are debriefed.

questions.text: The 3Rs of animal research are replacement, reduction and ___.
questions.explanation: Refinement means changing procedures to minimise suffering (Russell & Burch, 1959).

questions.text: Thinking about how research findings could be used to discriminate against a group is part of social ___.
questions.explanation: Psychologists must consider the wider impact of how findings are communicated and applied.

questions.prompt: Match each ethical guideline to its meaning.

pairs.right: Agreeing after knowing what is involved
Data cannot be linked to individuals
Leaving at any time without penalty
Explaining true aims after the study

questions.explanation: These guidelines protect participants' dignity and well-being.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of "replacement" in animal research?
options: Using computer models or cell cultures instead of animals
questions.explanation: Replacement swaps animals for alternatives; reduction uses fewer; refinement reduces suffering.

questions.prompt: A researcher reports that one ethnic group scores lower on a test without discussing test bias or environment. Which concept is most at stake?
questions.explanation: Reporting group differences without context can cause harm; psychologists have a social responsibility.

questions.prompt: Put these ethical steps in the order they happen in a study.
questions.explanation: Approval comes before recruiting; debriefing comes at the end.
